facts.text: Octopuses have three hearts.
Properly stored honey does not spoil.
A day on Venus is longer than its year.
Botanically, a banana is a berry.
Most snail shells coil to the right (dextral).
Wombats leave cube-shaped droppings.
A giraffe's very long neck has just seven neck bones; each one is long.
Axolotls can regrow body parts, including limbs.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
Sea otters use rocks to open shells.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal.
The blue whale is the largest animal on Earth.
A narwhal's long tusk is really a tooth.
Koalas can sleep up to 20 hours a day.
The elephant is the largest living land animal.
Arctic terns make one of the longest migrations of any animal.
The emperor penguin is the tallest and heaviest penguin.
Flamingos get their pink colour from carotenoids in their food.
Male seahorses carry the eggs in a brood pouch.
Tardigrades have survived exposure to outer space.
Some bamboos are among the fastest-growing plants in the world.
Young sunflowers turn their heads to follow the Sun.
Coast redwoods are the tallest living trees.
The Venus flytrap is a plant that catches insects.
The sensitive plant folds its leaves when touched.
The titan arum has the largest tuber of any known flowering plant.
A strawberry is an accessory fruit; its seeds sit on the outside.
A pineapple is a multiple fruit, formed from many small fruits joined together.
A coconut is a fruit called a drupe.
Pando is a forest of quaking aspen trees that grew from one root system.
The ginkgo tree is often called a living fossil.
Cactus spines are modified leaves.
Rafflesia arnoldii makes the largest single flower in the world.
Great Basin bristlecone pines can live for thousands of years.
Many trees add one growth ring each year, so the rings can show a tree's age.
Your heart is about the size of your fist.
An adult human has 206 bones.
The femur, in the thigh, is the longest bone in the human body.
Stomach acid contains hydrochloric acid.
The human brain has about 86 billion neurons.
The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the human body.
A red blood cell lives for about 120 days.
Fingerprint patterns are unique to each individual.
Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
The stapes, deep in the ear, is the smallest bone in the body.
The cornea, the clear front of the eye, has no blood vessels.
Hair is made mostly of a protein called keratin.
Taste buds detect tastes including bitterness, sweetness and savoriness (umami).
Your lungs bring oxygen into the body and carry carbon dioxide out.
Blood is made of blood cells suspended in a liquid called plasma.
The Rosetta Stone carries one text in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek scripts.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure for over 3,000 years.
The Terracotta Army is a collection of clay soldier statues buried with an emperor of China.
Johannes Gutenberg introduced the printing press to Europe around 1440.
Magna Carta was sealed in England in 1215.
Machu Picchu is an Inca citadel high in the Andes mountains of Peru.
The first ancient Olympic Games are traditionally dated to 776 BC.
Norse people built a settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Canada about 1,000 years ago.
The Silk Road was a network of trade routes linking East and West.
Easter Island is home to more than 900 giant stone statues called moai.
Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922.
Angkor Wat in Cambodia is the largest religious monument in the world.
Stonehenge has an outer ring of tall standing stones, called sarsens.
The Colosseum in Rome is the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built.
The Great Library of Alexandria was one of the largest libraries of the ancient world.
Hadrian's Wall was a Roman defensive wall in Britain, begun in AD 122.
Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree.
Many kinds of potato are grown in the Andes region of South America.
Saffron is one of the most expensive spices in the world by weight.
Vanilla is a spice that comes from orchids.
A peanut is a legume crop, grown mainly for its edible seeds.
After plain water, tea is the most widely consumed drink in the world.
Maple syrup is a sweet syrup made from the sap of maple trees.
Chili peppers get their heat from a chemical called capsaicin.
Popcorn pops because heated water inside the kernel turns to steam.
Coffee beans are the seeds of a fruit called the coffee cherry.
Early carrots were often purple or yellow, not orange.
Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world's people.
A pretzel is made from dough that is commonly shaped into a knot.
Sushi is a traditional Japanese dish made with vinegared rice.
Cheese is made by curdling milk, usually from cows, goats or sheep.
Cinnamon is a spice made from the inner bark of certain trees.
Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, at about 8,849 metres.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
Lake Baikal in Russia is the deepest lake in the world.
Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent.
The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth.
The Amazon is the largest rainforest in the world.
Auroras are bands of coloured light that glow in the sky near the poles.
The Dead Sea is so salty that people float easily in it.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall.
Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat in the world.
The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world.
Pangaea is the most recent supercontinent to have existed.
In a rainbow, sunlight separates into different colours inside raindrops.
Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.
Russia is the largest country in the world by area.
The word geyser comes from Geysir, a hot spring in Iceland.
The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean on Earth.
The Mariana Trench is the deepest oceanic trench on Earth.
The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system.
The whale shark is the largest known living fish.
The Sargasso Sea is the only named sea without land boundaries.
Kelp forests are underwater areas crowded with kelp.
Clownfish live safely among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones.
Many deep-sea animals make their own light, called bioluminescence.
Male humpback whales produce complex songs in the winter breeding season.
The orca is the largest member of the dolphin family.
Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow in shallow seawater.
A coral is a colony of many identical tiny animals called polyps.
Ocean tides are caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun.
Giant oceanic manta rays can be about 7 metres across.
The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's five oceans.
The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean on Earth.
Alexander Graham Bell was awarded the first US patent for a telephone in 1876.
In an incandescent bulb, a heated filament gives off the light.
Paper-like material has been found in China from the 2nd century BCE.
Whitcomb Judson patented an early zipper-like fastener in the 1890s.
Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.
In Japan, people gather under cherry blossoms in spring to enjoy them, a custom called hanami.
Post-it notes use a low-tack glue that lets them stick and peel off easily.
Most pencil cores are made of graphite powder mixed with clay.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
Alessandro Volta built the first electric battery, the voltaic pile, around 1800.
The stethoscope was invented by the French doctor René Laennec in 1816.
The LEGO company began in 1932 in Denmark.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web.
The microwave oven was developed after Percy Spencer noticed radar waves heating food.
Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656.
Walter Hunt invented the safety pin in 1849.
Hans Lippershey made the earliest known patent application for a telescope.
Elisha Otis showed his safety elevator in New York in 1854.
The Wright brothers made the first powered flights in 1903.
The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre museum in Paris.
Johannes Vermeer painted Girl with a Pearl Earring.
Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889.
Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the early 1500s.
Hokusai made The Great Wave off Kanagawa as a woodblock print.
Pablo Picasso painted Guernica in 1937.
The Bayeux Tapestry is about 70 metres long.
Origami is the art of folding paper.
Frida Kahlo painted many self-portraits.
A mosaic is a picture made from many small pieces called tesserae.
Kintsugi is a Japanese art of mending broken pottery with gold.
The Statue of Liberty is made of copper over an iron frame.
Michelangelo carved his statue David from a single block of marble.
Rembrandt's The Night Watch is kept in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
Stained glass windows are made from pieces of coloured glass.
Ukiyo-e is a Japanese art style whose name means "pictures of the floating world".
The Lascaux cave in France has over 600 wall paintings.
L. L. Zamenhof created the language Esperanto in the 1880s.
Papua New Guinea has more than 800 languages.
Braille letters are made from patterns of raised dots.
The Hawaiian alphabet has just thirteen letters.
The Rotokas language has one of the world's smallest sets of consonants.
Basque is a language isolate, unrelated to any other living language.
On La Gomera, people use a whistled language called Silbo Gomero.
"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" uses every letter of the alphabet.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards.
Christopher Latham Sholes helped design the QWERTY keyboard layout.
Sign languages use the visual-manual modality to convey meaning, not sound.
Sequoyah created a writing system for the Cherokee language in the 1820s.
Words like "buzz" and "splash" are onomatopoeia: they sound like what they name.
The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters.
The interrobang is a punctuation mark that combines a question mark and an exclamation mark.
The ampersand (&) began as a way to write the Latin word "et", meaning "and".
Mercury circles the Sun every 88 Earth days, faster than any other planet.
Mercury has no air to hold heat, so nights can drop to about -290 F.
Mercury is a little more than one third the width of Earth.
Sunlight takes about 3.2 minutes to reach Mercury.
Venus is the hottest planet, about 872 F at the surface, hot enough to melt lead.
The air pressure at the surface of Venus is about 93 times that at Earth's sea level.
Winds at the tops of Venus's clouds have been measured as high as 224 mph.
Venus takes 584 days to go through all its phases, while our Moon takes about a month.
Earth takes 365.25 days to go once around the Sun, so calendars need leap years.
Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees from its orbit plane, which gives us seasons.
Earth's oceans gave life a place to begin about 3.8 billion years ago.
One rotation of Earth takes 23.9 hours, a little less than 24.
Mars is about half the size of Earth.
A Martian day is called a sol and lasts 24.6 hours.
A year on Mars lasts 669.6 sols, the same as 687 Earth days.
Sunlight needs about 13 minutes to reach Mars.
If Jupiter were a hollow shell, 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.
Jupiter has the shortest day in the solar system, about 9.9 hours.
One year on Jupiter is about 12 Earth years.
A day on Saturn lasts only 10.7 hours.
Saturn's main rings span up to 175,000 miles but are typically only about 30 feet thick.
Saturn takes about 29.4 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.
The Cassini Division, a gap 2,920 miles wide, separates Saturn's A and B rings.
Uranus spins nearly sideways, at about a 90-degree angle to its orbit.
William Herschel found Uranus in 1781 and first thought it was a comet or a star.
One year on Uranus is about 84 Earth years.
Neptune finished its first orbit since its discovery in 2011, after 165 years.
Neptune was the first planet found by mathematical prediction, not by looking.
Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune, and Earth's daylight is about 900 times brighter.
Apollo astronauts brought back 842 pounds of lunar rocks and soil.
More than 105 robotic spacecraft have been launched to explore the Moon.
Humans first saw the far side of the Moon in 1959, from a Soviet spacecraft.
The Moon is on average 238,855 miles from Earth.
The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth.
New moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days.
The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth.
The Sun's core is about 27 million F, hot enough for nuclear fusion.
The Sun spins once in 25 Earth days at its equator but 36 days at its poles.
The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a disk of gas and dust.
The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
The space station makes 16 orbits a day, so its crew sees 16 sunrises and sunsets.
People have lived aboard the space station continuously since November 2000.
The station's solar array wingspan, 356 feet, beats an Airbus A380's 262 feet.
GPS is a system of more than 30 navigation satellites circling Earth.
The first satellite picture of Earth was taken by Explorer 6 on August 14, 1959.
TIROS-1 sent the first TV picture of Earth from space in 1960.
NASA's Aqua satellite launched May 4, 2002 with six Earth-observing instruments.
CloudSat was planned for 22 months of cloud radar but worked for over 17 years.
CloudSat carried a 94-GHz radar to see the vertical structure of clouds from space.
Landsat satellites have imaged Earth's land since 1972.
Landsat's free data added an estimated $25.6 billion to the US economy in 2023.
Landsat's archive shows how cities grew, coasts shifted, and forests changed since the 1970s.
About 30 percent of incoming sunlight is reflected back to space.
A cumulonimbus cloud can have a top reaching about 10 km (33,000 feet) or more.
Satellites only detect about 25 percent of fires burning worldwide, but those are the largest ones.
In 1998, smoke from fires in southern Mexico cut visibility to 2 km in parts of Texas.
About 90 percent of aerosols, by mass, come from natural sources.
Dust from North Africa can spread across the Atlantic Ocean, as seen in satellite imagery.
Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface would be about 0 F, not 59 F.
Roughly 30 percent of sunlight is reflected into space by clouds and ice.
Carbon dioxide levels rose nearly 38 percent between about 1750 and 2009.
Most ozone sits in the stratosphere, 10 to 40 km up, shielding us from ultraviolet rays.
An ozone molecule is made of three oxygen atoms.
The ocean's biological carbon pump moves about 10 gigatonnes of carbon to the deep sea yearly.
Global sea level rose between 10 and 25 cm during the 20th century.
Coastal populations were about 23 percent of the world's people in 1990.
Volcanic sulfate aerosols from Pinatubo in 1991 warmed the tropical stratosphere by 4 kelvin.
About 96.5 percent of Earth's water is in the global oceans.
Only a thousandth of one percent of Earth's water is water vapor in the air.
Earth holds about 1.39 billion cubic kilometers of water.
Evaporation from oceans and lakes supplies nearly 90 percent of the moisture in our air.
In the last 800,000 years there have been eight cycles of ice ages and warm periods.
The last ice age ended about 11,700 years ago.
Scientists showed the heat-trapping nature of carbon dioxide in the mid-19th century.
Titan is nearly 50 percent wider than Earth's Moon.
Christiaan Huygens discovered Saturn's moon Titan on March 25, 1655.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Pluto is about 3.6 billion miles from the Sun.
Giuseppe Piazzi spotted Ceres, the first asteroid belt object found, in 1801.
When Dawn arrived in 2015, Ceres became the first dwarf planet visited by a spacecraft.
Comets are leftovers from the birth of the solar system about 4.6 billion years ago.
Vesta, the largest asteroid, is about 329 miles across.
More than 150 asteroids are known to have small companion moons.
The nearest known black hole, Gaia BH1, is about 1,500 light-years away.
The most massive black hole observed, TON 618, weighs 66 billion times the Sun.
Stars orbiting near the Milky Way's center proved it holds a supermassive black hole.
Hubble was launched on April 24, 1990.
Webb orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, at a point called L2.
Webb has a 5-layer sunshield to block infrared from the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
Webb can see back over 13.5 billion years to the first galaxies after the Big Bang.
Hubble orbits 560 kilometers above Earth.
Parker Solar Probe will come within about 3.9 million miles of the Sun.
Parker Solar Probe was planned to make 24 orbits of the Sun over seven years.
Juno's first orbit of Jupiter stretched across 53 days.
Saturn was Cassini's home for 13 years.
New Horizons reached the Kuiper belt object Arrokoth in 2019.
New Horizons was the first spacecraft to explore Pluto up close, on July 14, 2015.
Perseverance passed Opportunity's Mars driving record of 28.06 miles.
Perseverance launched on July 30, 2020 to look for signs of ancient microbial life on Mars.
Curiosity climbed 1 kilometer in elevation up Mount Sharp, starting from Gale Crater.
Ingenuity was meant for five test flights but completed 72 flights over nearly three years.
On April 19, 2021 Ingenuity flew the first powered, controlled flight on Mars.
The Kepler space telescope launched on March 6, 2009.
Kepler's telescope had a 1-meter aperture and the largest digital camera sent to space then.
TESS has found nearly 6,000 confirmed or candidate exoplanets as of September 2025.
DART hit Dimorphos, a moonlet just 530 feet across, on September 26, 2022.
Dimorphos orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos, which is 2,560 feet across.
OSIRIS-REx collected rocks and dust from asteroid Bennu on October 20, 2020.
Europa Clipper is traveling 1.8 billion miles to reach Jupiter in April 2030.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, carrying Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins.
The Oort Cloud lies between 5,000 and 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun.
At a million miles a day, Voyager 1 will not reach the Oort Cloud for about 300 years.
The Perseid meteors are pieces of comet Swift-Tuttle, which swings by the Sun every 135 years.
Our solar system takes about 230 million years to orbit the center of the galaxy.
The solar system moves around the galaxy at about 515,000 mph.
Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in August 2012.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune.
Sunspot numbers rise and fall in a natural 11-year cycle.
Sunspots typically stretch 1,000 to 100,000 miles across.
One high tide to the next takes a little over 12 hours.
